text: Sanduk Ruit, a Nepali ophthalmologist born on September 4, 1954, in the remote mountainous village of Olangchunggola near the Tibet border, grew up in a village of 200 people located 11,000 feet above sea level on the lap of Mt. Kanchenjunga, one of the world's most isolated regions with no electricity, schools, health facilities, or modern communication, and snow-covered for six to nine months annually. His parents, Sonam and Kesang Ruit, were rural and illiterate, and he was the second of six children; he lost three siblings—his elder brother to diarrhoea at age three and his younger sister Chundak to fever at age eight—while his younger sister Yangla, who died at 15 from tuberculosis due to poverty, deeply influenced his decision to become a doctor to serve the poor. The nearest school was fifteen days’ walk away, and at age seven, his father sent him to St Robert's School in Darjeeling, where he stayed for four to five years before returning to Nepal. He graduated from Siddhartha Vanasthali School in Kathmandu in 1969 and later earned a Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery from King George's Medical College, Lucknow, with a scholarship from 1972 to 1976. He worked as a General Physician at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu for three years before specializing in ophthalmology, earning a Master’s Degree from the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi, in 1984. He worked at Tripureshwor Eye Hospital for eight years and, in 1986, was mentored by Australian ophthalmologist Fred Hollows, who recognized his dedication and offered him further training in Australia, the Netherlands, and the United States. In Australia, Ruit and Hollows developed Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS) using intraocular lenses, and Ruit became the first Nepali doctor to use them. To make surgeries more affordable, he established the Nepal Eye Program Australia, later renamed The Fred Hollows Foundation. Despite being offered a position in Australia, he returned to Nepal and continued working at Tripureshwor. In 1994, he founded the Tilganga Eye Center, now known as the Tilganga Institute of Ophthalmology, which produces intraocular lenses at less than US $5 each and prosthetic eyes for US $3 (compared to $150 for imports), and has performed over 100,000 operations, trained over 500 medical personnel globally, and works with the Himalayan Cataract Project, co-founded with Geoff Tabin, to provide free cataract surgeries in remote areas, often using mobile eye camps in tents, classrooms, or animal stables. Ruit restored the sight of over 180,000 people across Africa and Asia using SICS. His method, which has a 98% success rate at six months, is now taught in U.S. medical schools and uses lenses that are significantly cheaper than previous ones, developed in 1995. In 2006, after treating a North Korean diplomat in Kathmandu, he was invited to North Korea, where he conducted surgery on 1,000 patients and trained local surgeons. In April 2021, he launched the Tej Kohli & Ruit Foundation with a mission to screen 1,000,000 people and cure 300,000 of cataract blindness by 2026. The foundation conducted its first microsurgical outreach camp in Lumbini in March 2021, screening 1,387 patients and curing 312 cases of blindness, and another camp in Solukhumbu in April 2021, screening 1,214 patients and curing 178 cases. Ruit was awarded the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Peace and International Understanding for placing Nepal at the forefront of developing safe, effective, and economical cataract surgery procedures, enabling the needlessly blind in poor countries to see again, and the ISA award, the highest civilian honor in Bahrain, for developing affordable and sustainable cataract treatments with a cash prize of 1 million dollars. He is referred to as the "God of Sight" after restoring the sight of a 60-year-old woman in Indonesia. His biography, *The Barefoot Surgeon* by Ali Gripper, was published in June 2018, and a Nepali translation, *Sanduk Ruit*, was released by Fine Print Books in 2019. Ruit married Nanda Shrestha, an ophthalmic nurse, in 1987 and has one son and two daughters.
